summary: Miqyas logged 74 articles between Nov 21 and Nov 27, and the political category carried the week's heaviest negative weight: 15 of 74 political readings (20.3%) were negative against 10 positive (13.5%). That weight was concentrated. Every one of the 15 stories flagged for review this week was a political story rated negative, and nearly all of them trace to two linked confrontations: a dispute inside the governing coalition about creating new provinces, and an escalating standoff between Punjab authorities and the JUI-F. The economic picture ran the other way. Economic readings were 79.7% neutral, with positives (14.9%) nearly triple the negatives (5.4%), helped by government cuts to kerosene, jet fuel and light diesel oil prices on Nov 21 and a diesel price that fell below Rs350 on Nov 26 for the first time in four months, as reported. The few economic negatives were operational: a petroleum dealers' strike warning and a conveyor belt failure that disrupted coal imports at a bulk terminal.

The new provinces row was the week's dominant storyline, and it unfolded as a chain of public exchanges. On Nov 22, PPP Senator Sherry Rehman urged the government to put people's problems ahead of divisive moves, after Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari's warnings against dividing Sindh drew sharp replies from PML-N ministers. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi then publicly warned an unnamed minister about his criticism; PM's adviser Rana Sanaullah answered that he would not be intimidated and accused Naqvi of mishandling the debate; and by Nov 25 Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had told ministers to stop attacking each other in public. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar ended the week challenging Bilawal's opposition to a referendum on new provinces, while saying differences had not broken party ties; the same report notes that no referendum proposal exists. A related thread came via a Senate subcommittee, whose convener said Punjab holds about 60pc of senior federal secretariat posts and called that a constitutional violation, a claim reported without a government rebuttal.

The second cluster concerns civil liberties and the limits of state power. Under the emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, President Zardari issued ordinances on Nov 22 withdrawing most privileges of provincial lawmakers, including protection against preventive detention, and creating centrally nominated committees shielded from civil courts. In Punjab, the JUI-F petitioned the Lahore High Court alleging that party chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman had been confined to his Lahore home, which police described as a request to limit his movement; the court ordered a police report on Nov 26. The party then said senior leaders had been arrested in Khushab and, on Nov 27, that Fazl himself had been detained, which a senior police officer denied. These stories help explain the social category's 17.6% negative share, as several involved road closures, raids or curbs on assembly, and Karachi was placed on high alert ahead of planned rallies. Even so, social coverage posted the week's highest positive share at 23.0%. A former IHC judge's warning that the 26th and 27th amendments have pitted two superior courts against each other added an institutional dimension to the week.

On lean, the readings held steady despite charged material: 67 of 74 articles were rated balanced, 5 pro-government and 2 pro-opposition. Both pro-opposition ratings went to JUI-F stories built mainly on the party's own account, which reflects how those reports were sourced. Confidence is the more telling signal. Across the week 26 articles were rated high confidence, but among the 15 flagged stories only 2 were, with 12 medium and 1 low. The low rating went to the competing claims about Fazl's arrest, where the party and the police gave directly conflicting accounts with no independent verification. The week's most dramatic political claims should be read as attributed and, in several cases, still unconfirmed. One caveat on coverage: Nov 21 produced no flagged stories, so the flagged set spans Nov 22 to Nov 27.

notableStories.headline: Presidential ordinance withdraws most privileges of KP MPAs, including protection against preventive detention
notableStories.context: Under emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, five presidential ordinances stripped provincial lawmakers of most privileges, including immunity from preventive detention, and set up centrally nominated committees shielded from civil courts.

notableStories.headline: PM urges ministers to avoid spat amid Sanaullah-Naqvi row over new provinces
notableStories.context: The new provinces debate escalated into public sparring between senior government figures, prompting Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to tell ministers to stop attacking each other.

notableStories.headline: Punjab holds over 60pc of senior federal posts, Senate body told
notableStories.context: A Senate subcommittee convener called Punjab's reported share of about 60pc of senior federal posts a constitutional violation and sought a correction plan, feeding the week's wider argument about provincial balance.

notableStories.headline: Lahore High Court seeks police report on Maulana Fazl's confinement
notableStories.context: The court ordered Lahore's police chief to respond to the JUI-F's claim that its chief was being held at his residence, a dispute that later produced conflicting accounts of an arrest.

notableStories.headline: 26th, 27th Amendments sparked judicial conflict: ex-IHC judge
notableStories.context: Former IHC judge Mohsin Akhtar Kayani said the two constitutional amendments have set superior courts against each other and urged parliament to resolve it, while also criticising PECA notices to media.
